# Zvarsity: ELSS Funds

**Duration:** 7 minutes | **Level:** Beginner

## An Equity Fund With a Tax Deduction Attached

Most equity mutual funds are just that — funds that invest in equity, with no special tax treatment beyond the standard LTCG/STCG rules covered in the **Capital Gains Tax** lesson. **ELSS (Equity-Linked Savings Scheme)** funds are a specific category that comes with an extra feature bolted on: investing in them can reduce your taxable income *today*, under a specific section of the Income Tax Act, in exchange for agreeing to leave the money invested for a minimum period.

That trade — a tax deduction now, in exchange for a lock-in — is the entire identity of ELSS as a category. This lesson covers what an ELSS fund actually is, how the lock-in works (including a nuance that trips up a lot of SIP investors), the deduction itself, and how ELSS compares conceptually to other common tax-saving options.

---

## What Is an ELSS Fund?

An ELSS fund is, mechanically, an equity mutual fund — it invests predominantly in stocks, and it carries the market risk and return potential of equity investing like any other equity fund. What sets it apart is purely a tax-law label: because it qualifies under **Section 80C** of the Income Tax Act, investing in it lets you claim a deduction on your taxable income, and in exchange, the fund imposes a **mandatory 3-year lock-in** from the date of each investment.

Beyond the lock-in and the deduction, an ELSS fund behaves like any other diversified equity fund — its returns are driven by the performance of the stocks it holds, subject to the same LTCG/STCG tax treatment (12.5% on LTCG above ₹1,25,000/year, 20% on STCG) covered in earlier lessons once units are actually sold.

---

## The 3-Year Lock-In — and the SIP Nuance

Every rupee invested in an ELSS fund is locked in for **3 years from its date of investment**. You cannot redeem those units — no matter how much they've gained or lost — until the 3-year mark passes.

This is straightforward for a **lump-sum investment**: invest ₹50,000 on a single date, and that entire ₹50,000 (plus whatever it has grown to) unlocks on the same date 3 years later.

It gets more interesting with a **SIP (Systematic Investment Plan)** — investing a fixed amount every month. Here's the nuance that catches a lot of first-time ELSS investors off guard:

> **Each SIP installment has its own, independent 3-year lock-in window.** It is *not* the case that starting a SIP locks in the whole plan for 3 years from the first installment. Every single monthly installment is treated as a separate investment, with its own lock-in clock starting from the date *that specific installment* was made.

### Worked Example

An investor starts a monthly SIP of ₹5,000 into an ELSS fund on the 15th of each month, starting January 2024. Here's when a few of those installments actually unlock:

| Installment Date | Lock-In Ends |
|---|---|
| 15 Jan 2024 | 15 Jan 2027 |
| 15 Feb 2024 | 15 Feb 2027 |
| 15 Mar 2024 | 15 Mar 2027 |
| ... | ... |
| 15 Dec 2026 | 15 Dec 2029 |

By early 2027, the investor's very first installments start becoming redeemable — but installments made later are still locked in, each unlocking exactly 3 years after it was invested. If this investor stops the SIP and wants to redeem everything at once, they'd find that only the older installments are actually available; the more recent ones are still inside their individual lock-in windows. Planning around ELSS liquidity means thinking in terms of *each installment's own clock*, not one single date for the whole SIP.

---

## The Section 80C Deduction — Old Regime Only

The reason ELSS exists as a distinct fund category is **Section 80C** of the Income Tax Act, which allows a deduction of up to **₹1,50,000 per financial year** from taxable income for a defined list of eligible investments and expenses — ELSS is one of them, alongside things like PPF, life insurance premiums, and principal repayment on a home loan, among others.

Here is the point most likely to cause confusion, and it deserves to be stated plainly:

> ⚠️ **The Section 80C deduction — including for ELSS — is available only under the OLD tax regime.** The **NEW tax regime**, which has been the default regime since FY 2023-24 unless a taxpayer actively chooses to opt for the old regime instead, does **not** allow the 80C deduction at all.

This means the tax-saving pitch behind ELSS — "invest and reduce your taxable income by up to ₹1,50,000" — simply doesn't apply if you're filing under the new regime, which is now most taxpayers by default. Before investing in ELSS specifically *for* the 80C benefit, it's worth confirming which regime you're actually filing under, since choosing (or defaulting into) the new regime removes the deduction entirely — the fund still exists and can still be invested in as a plain equity fund, but the tax-saving reason for choosing it over any other equity fund disappears under the new regime.

---

## How ELSS Compares to Other 80C Options

ELSS is one of several instruments that qualify for the 80C deduction (under the old regime), but they are far from interchangeable — the lock-in length and the underlying asset class differ sharply:

| | ELSS | PPF (Public Provident Fund) |
|---|---|---|
| **Asset class** | Equity (market-linked, variable returns) | Government-backed debt instrument |
| **Lock-in** | 3 years (shortest among common 80C options) | Much longer — a multi-year lock-in measured in over a decade |
| **Return character** | Variable, tied to equity market performance | Fixed/declared periodically by the government |
| **80C eligible** | Yes (old regime only) | Yes (old regime only) |

The point of this comparison isn't that one is "better" — it's that they serve different roles. ELSS has by far the shortest lock-in among common 80C instruments, and its equity exposure means it carries market risk in exchange for higher long-term return potential. PPF and similar debt-oriented options trade a much longer lock-in for government-backed stability and predictability. This lesson intentionally does not state current PPF interest rates or exact PPF tenure figures, since these are set and revised by the government periodically — check current, official figures before comparing precisely.

---

## A Brief Note on Rules Changing

Tax law — including the 80C list, deduction limits, and which regime is the default — is set by the government and can change from one budget to the next. Treat the figures in this lesson as a snapshot of the rules as of FY 2026-27 (AY 2027-28), not a permanent guarantee — check the latest Union Budget for any change to these specific rules, and confirm current figures with a qualified tax professional or chartered accountant before making a filing decision based on them.

---

## Key Terms

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **ELSS (Equity-Linked Savings Scheme)** | An equity mutual fund category that qualifies for Section 80C deduction, with a mandatory 3-year lock-in |
| **Lock-In Period** | The minimum time units must be held before redemption is allowed |
| **Section 80C** | Income Tax Act provision allowing deductions up to ₹1,50,000/year for eligible investments — old tax regime only |
| **Old Tax Regime** | The tax regime that permits deductions like 80C, opted into rather than default |
| **New Tax Regime** | The default regime since FY 2023-24; does not allow the 80C deduction |
| **SIP (Systematic Investment Plan)** | Fixed periodic investment; in ELSS, each installment carries its own independent 3-year lock-in |

---

## Takeaway

✅ ELSS is an equity mutual fund that qualifies for a Section 80C deduction in exchange for a mandatory 3-year lock-in.
✅ For SIP investments, each monthly installment has its own independent 3-year lock-in — not one lock-in for the whole SIP.
✅ Section 80C allows deductions up to ₹1,50,000/year — but only under the old tax regime; the new regime (the default since FY 2023-24) does not allow it.
✅ Beyond the lock-in and deduction, ELSS follows the same LTCG/STCG tax rules as any other equity investment once units are sold.
✅ Compared to other 80C options like PPF, ELSS has a much shorter lock-in but carries equity market risk instead of government-backed stability — confirm current details with a tax professional before deciding.

**Next lesson:** "Options Trading Basics" — an introduction to a different corner of the markets entirely.

quiz.question: What is the mandatory lock-in period for a lump-sum investment in an ELSS fund?
options: There is no lock-in for ELSS
quiz.explanation: ELSS funds carry a mandatory 3-year lock-in from the date of investment, the shortest lock-in among common Section 80C-eligible options.

quiz.question: An investor runs a monthly SIP into an ELSS fund for 2 years and then stops. How does the lock-in apply to the accumulated units?
options: The entire SIP is locked in for 3 years starting from the very first installment only
Each monthly installment has its own independent 3-year lock-in, starting from that installment's own investment date
SIP investments in ELSS have no lock-in at all
The lock-in only applies to the final installment
quiz.explanation: Each SIP installment in an ELSS fund is treated as a separate investment with its own 3-year lock-in clock — not one lock-in date for the whole SIP.

quiz.question: Under which tax regime can an investor claim the Section 80C deduction for an ELSS investment?
options: Both the old and new tax regimes equally
Only the old tax regime — the new tax regime does not allow the 80C deduction
quiz.explanation: The Section 80C deduction, including for ELSS, is available only under the old tax regime. The new tax regime, the default since FY 2023-24, does not permit this deduction.

quiz.question: What is the maximum deduction available under Section 80C per financial year (old regime)?
quiz.explanation: Section 80C allows deductions up to ₹1,50,000 per financial year for eligible investments and expenses, including ELSS — but only under the old tax regime.

quiz.question: How does ELSS's lock-in generally compare to PPF's lock-in?
options: ELSS has a much longer lock-in than PPF
ELSS's 3-year lock-in is considerably shorter than PPF's much longer, multi-year lock-in
PPF has no lock-in at all
quiz.explanation: ELSS has one of the shortest lock-ins among 80C-eligible instruments at 3 years, while PPF carries a much longer lock-in measured in well over a decade, trading liquidity for government-backed stability.
